components.note: 氵 (water) — relates directly to 流's meaning 'to flow.'
㐬 (liú) gives the sound — 流 is also pronounced liú, an exact match.
皿 (a vessel) — a chalice or bowl
丿 — a single drop of blood inside the vessel

example.hanzi: 他的手流血了。
example.pinyin: Tā de shǒu liúxuè le.
example.english: His hand is bleeding.
example.fact: 流血 is a verb-object compound (流 "flow" + 血 "blood" as its object), and like many VO compounds it can take an aspect marker two ways: attached to the end of the whole phrase (流血了, "bled") or inserted between the verb and its object (流了血) — a flexibility ordinary single-morpheme verbs don't have.

components.note: 儿 (a person) — shown carrying a torch overhead, the source of 光's meaning 'light, brightness.'
火 (fire) — the torch's flame, the thing giving off the light.

example.hanzi: 欢迎光临我们的新店。
example.pinyin: Huānyíng guānglín wǒmen de xīn diàn.
example.english: Welcome to our new store.
example.fact: 光临 is an honorific built from 光 ("light, radiance") plus 临 ("to arrive") — literally elevating a guest's arrival into something luminous. It shows up almost exclusively in polite or commercial set phrases like 欢迎光临 (heard at shop entrances across China), never to describe an ordinary person just showing up.

components.note: 衤 (clothes) — 衬 names an item of clothing.
寸 (cùn) gives a sound distantly related to chèn, having drifted apart over time.
衤 (clothes) — 衫 names a piece of clothing, a shirt.
彡 (shān) gives the sound — an exact match with 衫.

example.hanzi: 他穿着一件白衬衫。
example.pinyin: Tā chuānzhe yí jiàn bái chènshān.
example.english: He is wearing a white shirt.
example.fact: 衬 means "to line, to serve as an underlayer," so 衬衫 literally frames the shirt as an inner layer of clothing. Its near-synonym 衬衣 swaps in 衣 ("garment") for 衫 ("shirt") with no change in meaning — one of several clothing words where the suffix varies by region or speaker without altering the word.

components.note: 金 depicts a bell or metal casting mold, with dots representing droplets of molten metal — a picture linked to metal and, later, specifically gold.

example.hanzi: 她有一头金发。
example.pinyin: Tā yǒu yì tóu jīnfà.
example.english: She has blond hair.
example.fact: The simplified character 发 merges two originally distinct traditional characters: 髮 (fà, "hair") and 發 (fā, "to send out, to develop"). 金发 uses the fà reading, but the identical simplified glyph in a word like 发展 ("to develop") is read fā — a common trap for learners who only know the simplified form.

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 摧 describes destroying something by force, by hand.
崔 (cuī) gives the sound — an exact match with 摧.
臼 pictures a clay mortar or vessel.
殳 (a tool, held in a hand) strikes it, giving 毁 its meaning 'to destroy, to smash.'

example.hanzi: 地震摧毁了这座城市。
example.pinyin: Dìzhèn cuīhuǐ le zhè zuò chéngshì.
example.english: The earthquake destroyed this city.
example.fact: 摧毁 doubles up two near-synonymous "destroy" morphemes (摧 "to break/crush" and 毁 "to ruin") into one intensified verb, the same synonym-stacking strategy behind 喜欢. It's reserved for large-scale, often irreversible destruction — buildings, cities, systems — where a smaller broken object would instead call for 弄坏 or 打破.

components.note: ⺼ (flesh) — 胳 names a body part.
各 (gè) gives a sound close to gē, sharing the same initial.
⺼ (flesh/body) — 膊 names a body part, the upper arm.
尃 (fū) gives a sound only distantly related to bó today, having drifted apart over time.

example.hanzi: 他的胳膊很疼。
example.pinyin: Tā de gēbo hěn téng.
example.english: His arm hurts a lot.
example.fact: Northern Mandarin speech tends to favor 胳膊 (gēbo) for "arm," while 手臂 (shǒubì, also in this batch) leans more common in southern speech and in formal or written registers — two regionally split words for the same body part, both still current in standard Mandarin today.

components.note: 亻 (person) plus 也 (also/additionally) — historically meant 'another person,' which developed into the third-person pronoun 'he/him.'
A simple line drawing of a person's legs seen from the side, used to depict a human being.

example.hanzi: 不要伤害他人。
example.pinyin: Búyào shānghài tārén.
example.english: Don't hurt other people.
example.fact: 他人 is the formal, written-register counterpart to the everyday spoken 别人 — both mean "other people," but 他人 turns up in legal text, proverbs, and set phrases, while 别人 dominates in casual conversation.

components.note: 我 (wǒ) reflects the character's phonetic root, though the sound has diverged over time from the modern reading é.
罒 (net) — relates to 罗's original meaning 'net for catching birds,' extended to 'to gather, collect' and used today as a common Chinese surname.

example.hanzi: 他去过俄罗斯三次。
example.pinyin: Tā qùguo Éluósī sān cì.
example.english: He has been to Russia three times.
example.fact: 俄罗斯 is a phonetic transliteration of "Russia" ultimately tracing back to the Slavic root "Rus'." Mongolian phonotactics don't allow words to start with an "r" sound, so an initial vowel was added somewhere along the borrowing path (compare Mongolian Oros) — one reason the Chinese name starts with 俄- rather than something closer to "Ru-."

meanings: pal (colloquial address for a close friend)
erhua form of 哥們|哥们[ge1 men5]

components.note: 哥 doubles the character 可 ('to approve, to sing'), originally suggesting a call-and-response song between two singers; the meaning later narrowed to 'elder brother.'
亻 (person) — 们 attaches to pronouns and nouns referring to people to mark plural, e.g. 我们 ('we'), 你们 ('you all')
门 (mén) gives a sound close to 们's reading (men)
儿 (simplified from 兒) depicts a small child, drawn with a large head on a small body — a simple picture of youth.

example.hanzi: 我们是好哥们儿。
example.pinyin: Wǒmen shì hǎo gēmenr.
example.english: We're good buddies.
example.fact: 哥们儿 builds on 哥 ("older brother"), extending brotherhood outward to close friends who aren't blood relatives. The r-suffixed erhua form marks it as distinctly colloquial, Beijing-flavored speech, compared to the plainer, more nationwide 哥们 without the 儿.

components.note: 异 (a simplified form of 異) depicts a person with upraised hands and an odd expression, suggesting something strange or different.
巾 (cloth) — 常 originally referred to a long skirt or banner made of cloth, later coming to mean something 'usual' or 'ordinary.'
尚 (shàng) gives a hint of the sound — 常 is pronounced cháng, a connection that has drifted over time.

example.hanzi: 他今天的行为很异常。
example.pinyin: Tā jīntiān de xíngwéi hěn yìcháng.
example.english: His behavior today is very unusual.
example.fact: 异常 does double duty as both an adjective ("abnormal") and, less obviously to learners, an intensifying adverb before another adjective (异常重要, "extremely important") — much like English "unusually" can mean either "in an unusual way" or simply "very."

components.note: 疒 (sickness) — 疾 names a disease or ailment.
矢 (shǐ) gives a sound distantly related to jí, having drifted apart over time.
疒 (sickness) — relates directly to 病's meaning 'illness, disease, to be sick.'
丙 (bǐng) gives a sound hint — 病 is pronounced bìng, sharing the same base sound with a different tone.

example.hanzi: 这种疾病很难治疗。
example.pinyin: Zhè zhǒng jíbìng hěn nán zhìliáo.
example.english: This disease is very difficult to treat.
example.fact: Classical commentary in the 说文解字 glosses 病 as an intensified 疾 ("病, 疾加也") — 疾 being the milder, earlier-stage ailment and 病 what it becomes once serious. Modern Mandarin has largely lost that distinction, and 疾病 just reinforces the two near-synonymous roots into one formal word for "disease."

components.note: 耳 (ear) — an old link between listening to official duties and 职's meaning 'duty, profession, office'
只 (zhī) gives a loose sound connection to 职's reading zhí
责 shows 贝 (money, a cowry shell) at its base, tied to a debt that must be repaid — giving 责 its meaning 'duty, responsibility, to blame.'

example.hanzi: 保护环境是我们的职责。
example.pinyin: Bǎohù huánjìng shì wǒmen de zhízé.
example.english: Protecting the environment is our responsibility.
example.fact: 职责 pairs 职 ("post, position," as in 职位) with 责 ("responsibility, blame") to name the duties attached to a specific job or role — distinct from the broader 责任 ("responsibility"), which doesn't require holding any official position at all.

components.note: 心 was originally a pictograph of the physical shape of a human heart, and came to represent the mind, feelings, and intention as well.
⺼ (flesh) shows 脏 (zàng) relates to the body, as in internal organs.
庄 (zhuāng) gives a sound close to zàng, sharing a similar consonant sound though the vowel and ending differ.
疒 (sickness) — relates directly to 病's meaning 'illness, disease, to be sick.'
丙 (bǐng) gives a sound hint — 病 is pronounced bìng, sharing the same base sound with a different tone.

example.hanzi: 他的爷爷得了心脏病。
example.pinyin: Tā de yéye dé le xīnzàngbìng.
example.english: His grandfather got heart disease.
example.fact: 心脏病 is fully transparent: 心脏 ("heart," literally "heart-organ") plus 病 ("disease"). Chinese medical vocabulary reuses this organ+病 template widely, e.g. 糖尿病 ("diabetes," literally "sugar-urine disease") and 皮肤病 ("skin disease").

components.note: 八 here depicts something splitting apart or being divided.
厶 is an old form meaning 'private' or 'one's own' — 公 shows dividing up private property to share it fairly, giving rise to the meaning 'public' or 'fair.'
人 (person), tripled — three people together depict a crowd, giving 众 its meaning 'many, multitude.'

example.hanzi: 这个消息已经向公众公开了。
example.pinyin: Zhège xiāoxi yǐjīng xiàng gōngzhòng gōngkāi le.
example.english: This news has already been made public.
example.fact: 公众 names the general public as a neutral collective (公众人物, "public figure"; 公众意见, "public opinion"), while the related word 群众 ("the masses") carries more of a political, revolutionary-era flavor of ordinary people as distinct from officials — two overlapping but not interchangeable "public" words.

components.note: 戈 (a dagger-axe, a weapon) — 战 relates to fighting and war.
占 (zhàn) gives the sound — 战 is also pronounced zhàn, an exact match.

example.hanzi: 这位战士在战争中受伤了。
example.pinyin: Zhè wèi zhànshì zài zhànzhēng zhōng shòushāng le.
example.english: This soldier was wounded in the war.
example.fact: 战士 combines 战 ("war, to fight") with 士, an old term for a warrior-scholar or gentleman-soldier in ancient Chinese society — the same 士 that shows up honorifically in 勇士 ("brave warrior") and 护士 ("nurse," literally "guarding-士").

components.note: 尸 (here representing a covering or stall, not a corpse) — 展 pictures a place where goods are displayed.
衣 (clothing) — clothing laid out for display gave 展 its meaning 'to unfold' or 'to exhibit.'
王 (a variant of 玉, meaning jade) — a valuable object one might glimpse or notice.
见 (to see) — catching sight of something links to the meanings 'to appear, present, now.'

example.hanzi: 这幅画展现了大自然的美。
example.pinyin: Zhè fú huà zhǎnxiàn le dà zìrán de měi.
example.english: This painting displays the beauty of nature.
example.fact: 展现 leans toward a vivid, often visual "unfolding" — a scene, a talent, a quality coming into view — while its near-synonym 展示 is more neutral and deliberate ("to demonstrate, to exhibit," as at a trade show): what a painting reveals calls for 展现, while what a presenter actively shows off calls for 展示.

components.note: 木 (wood) — buildings were traditionally framed with wood.
娄 (lóu) gives the sound — an exact match with 楼.
A short stroke placed below a longer one — the mirror image of 上 (up), together forming a simple, opposite pair.

example.hanzi: 我们在楼下等你。
example.pinyin: Wǒmen zài lóuxià děng nǐ.
example.english: We'll wait for you downstairs.
example.fact: 楼下 and its opposite 楼上 ("upstairs") both pair 楼 ("multi-story building/floor") with a plain directional word (下 "down," 上 "up") — one of Mandarin's most transparent compass-style compounds, mirroring how 里面/外面 and 前面/后面 pair a location noun with a directional opposite.

components.note: A drawing of a person standing with arms and legs spread wide — used to represent the idea of something being 'big' or 'great.'
里 (a unit of distance, related to a village measure) — 量 relates to measuring quantity.
旦 (dàn) gives a hint of the sound — 量 is pronounced liàng, a connection that has shifted significantly over time.

example.hanzi: 工厂每天生产大量的产品。
example.pinyin: Gōngchǎng měitiān shēngchǎn dàliàng de chǎnpǐn.
example.english: The factory produces a large quantity of products every day.
example.fact: 大量 almost always precedes a noun with 的 (大量的 + noun) to mean "a large quantity of," much like English "a lot of." On its own 量 already means "quantity, measure" (as in 数量, "amount"), making 大量 one of the more literal, transparent compounds in this batch.

components.note: 门 is a picture of a double-leafed door or gate, drawn symmetrically to show two swinging panels.
口 is a simple picture of an open mouth.

example.hanzi: 他站在门口等我。
example.pinyin: Tā zhàn zài ménkǒu děng wǒ.
example.english: He stood at the doorway waiting for me.
example.fact: 门口 literally combines 门 ("door, gate") with 口 ("mouth, opening") — the same 口 that marks an "opening" in 入口 ("entrance") and 出口 ("exit"), extending the body-part word for "mouth" into a general term for any threshold one passes through.

components.note: 讠 (speech) — the act of speaking.
正 (straight, correct) — speaking the straight, correct truth, giving 证 its meaning 'to prove, certify; evidence.'
讠 (speech) — 词 names a word, a unit of speech.
司 (sī) gives the sound — an exact match with 词.

example.hanzi: 证人在法庭上提供了证词。
example.pinyin: Zhèngrén zài fǎtíng shàng tígōng le zhèngcí.
example.english: The witness provided testimony in court.
example.fact: 证词 is a legal-register word combining 证 ("evidence, to prove," as in 证据 "evidence" and 证人 "witness") with 词 ("words, statement") — literally "evidentiary words," reserved for formal courtroom or legal contexts rather than an everyday claim someone makes.

components.note: 敕 (an order, discipline) — relates to 整's meaning 'orderly, whole, to arrange.'
正 (zhèng) gives a sound hint — 整 is pronounced zhěng, sharing the same base sound with a different tone.
王 (a variant form of 玉, meaning jade) — 理 originally referred to the natural grain or pattern in jade, later extending to 'reason, logic, to manage.'
里 (lǐ) gives the sound — 理 is also pronounced lǐ, an exact match.

example.hanzi: 我周末要整理房间。
example.pinyin: Wǒ zhōumò yào zhěnglǐ fángjiān.
example.english: I need to tidy my room this weekend.
example.fact: 整理 spans both a literal, physical "tidying up" (整理房间, "tidy the room") and an abstract "organizing" of information (整理数据, "collate data") — one verb covering the same physical-to-abstract range that English splits between "tidy" and "organize."

components.note: 木 (tree) is repeated three times, piling up to picture a dense forest.
木 (tree), doubled — two trees side by side depict a cluster of trees, the source of 林's meaning 'forest, grove.'

example.hanzi: 这座森林里有很多野生动物。
example.pinyin: Zhè zuò sēnlín lǐ yǒu hěn duō yěshēng dòngwù.
example.english: There are many wild animals in this forest.
example.fact: 森林 stacks two tree-pile pictographs: 木 ("tree") tripled into 森 ("dense forest") and 木 doubled into 林 ("grove, cluster of trees") — a visually literal compound where more repeated tree-strokes really do signal denser woodland, one of the clearest surviving pictographic logics in modern vocabulary.

components.note: 讠 (speech) — relates to 调's meaning 'to adjust, transfer,' something coordinated through spoken negotiation.
周 (zhōu) served as the phonetic base; its pronunciation has since drifted well away from diào.
尺 (a ruler/measure) — represents rules or measures being set.
口 (mouth) — measures being discussed aloud in one place gave 局 its meaning 'bureau, office, situation.'

example.hanzi: 联邦调查局正在调查这起案件。
example.pinyin: Liánbāng Diàochájú zhèngzài diàochá zhè qǐ ànjiàn.
example.english: The Federal Bureau of Investigation is investigating this case.
example.fact: 调查局 simply appends 局 ("bureau, office" — the same 局 in 邮局 "post office" and 警察局 "police station") onto 调查 ("to investigate"), giving a transparent "investigation bureau." It's most familiar as the last three characters of 联邦调查局, the standard Chinese name for the American FBI.

components.note: 弓 (bow) — a strong bow that took great force to draw gave 强 its meaning 'strong, powerful.'
虫 was a different phonetic element historically; its pronunciation has shifted so far from qiáng over time that the sound link is no longer obvious.
辶 (to walk) — pressing close on someone's heels ties to 迫's meaning 'to press, to force.'
白 (bái) gives a sound distantly related to pò, having drifted apart over time.

example.hanzi: 别强迫孩子学他们不喜欢的东西。
example.pinyin: Bié qiǎngpò háizi xué tāmen bù xǐhuan de dōngxi.
example.english: Don't force children to learn things they don't like.
example.fact: 强迫 combines 强 ("strong, forceful") with 迫 ("to press, to pressure," as in 迫切 "urgent") — both halves already lean toward coercion on their own. The word commonly appears in the passive construction 被强迫 ("to be forced to").

components.note: 氵 (water) — 注 relates to pouring or directing, like water poured into something
主 (zhǔ) gives a sound close to 注's reading zhù
宀 (roof) — represents a home or fixed dwelling.
疋 (a foot/person) — a person settling down under a roof gave 定 its meaning 'to decide, to fix, to settle.'

example.hanzi: 他们的爱情注定要失败。
example.pinyin: Tāmen de àiqíng zhùdìng yào shībài.
example.english: Their love was destined to fail.
example.fact: 注定 leans on 定 ("fixed, settled") plus 注 (roughly "to inscribe, to note down," as in an official record) — together suggesting fate has already been written down and fixed. The word itself is neutral about good or bad outcomes; only context makes it sound like "doomed" rather than simply "destined."

components.note: 日 (sun) — 暗 describes the absence of light, the opposite of a bright sun.
音 (yīn) reflects the character's historical phonetic root, though the modern reading àn has diverged.
A pictograph of an altar or offering table used in ancestor worship — presenting offerings extended to 示's meaning 'to show, display, indicate.'

example.hanzi: 她的话暗示了她并不高兴。
example.pinyin: Tā de huà ànshì le tā bìng bù gāoxìng.
example.english: Her words hinted that she wasn't happy at all.
example.fact: 暗示 literally means "dark/hidden (暗) indication (示)." Its opposite, 明示 ("to state explicitly"), swaps in 明 ("bright, clear") for 暗 — the same 示 root flips meaning entirely depending on which "light" character precedes it.

components.note: 手 is a simple picture of an open hand with the fingers spread out.
⺼ (flesh) shows 臂 relates to a part of the body.
辟 (pì) gives a sound close to bì, differing mainly in the initial consonant.

example.hanzi: 他伸出手臂拥抱了朋友。
example.pinyin: Tā shēnchū shǒubì yōngbào le péngyou.
example.english: He stretched out his arm to hug his friend.
example.fact: 手臂 pairs 手 ("hand") with 臂 ("arm") into one word for the whole limb, and it extends figuratively to mean a trusted assistant or "right-hand" helper — the same body-part metaphor English makes with the phrase "right-hand man."

components.note: 彳 (step/walk) — relates directly to 往's meaning 'to go toward, in the direction of.'
王 (wáng) gives a sound hint — 往 is pronounced wǎng, sharing the same base sound with a different tone.

example.hanzi: 代表团明天前往北京。
example.pinyin: Dàibiǎotuán míngtiān qiánwǎng Běijīng.
example.english: The delegation will head to Beijing tomorrow.
example.fact: 前往 is a formal, written-register word for "to go to," typical of news reports, itineraries, and official announcements. Everyday spoken Mandarin almost always reaches for the plain verb 去 instead, so hearing 前往 signals a noticeably more formal register.

components.note: 谷 (valley) — 豁 relates to an open gap or breach, like a valley cutting through terrain.
害 (hài) gives a sound distantly related to 豁's reading huō, having drifted apart over time.

example.hanzi: 外交官享有法律豁免权。
example.pinyin: Wàijiāoguān xiǎngyǒu fǎlǜ huòmiǎnquán.
example.english: Diplomats enjoy legal immunity.
example.fact: 豁免 is formal legal/administrative vocabulary, most often attached to 权 as 豁免权 ("immunity," e.g. diplomatic immunity). 豁 contributes a sense of "opening up, clearing away" (compare 豁达, "open-minded"), reinforcing 免's core meaning of being excused or exempted from something.

components.note: A simple line drawing of a person's legs seen from the side, used to depict a human being.

example.hanzi: 法官询问了案件的当事人。
example.pinyin: Fǎguān xúnwèn le ànjiàn de dāngshìrén.
example.english: The judge questioned the parties involved in the case.
example.fact: 当事人 is standard legal vocabulary for the parties directly involved in a case — literally "the person(s) at (当) the matter (事)." It deliberately stays neutral about role or guilt, unlike more specific legal terms such as 被告 ("defendant") or 原告 ("plaintiff").

components.note: 月 (yuè) here actually derives from 肉 (meat) — 有 originally depicted a hand holding meat, meaning 'to possess'; it also lends a loose phonetic connection to yǒu.
穴 (a cave/hole) — 空 relates to an empty hollow space.
工 (gōng) gives a hint of the sound — 空 is pronounced kōng, a connection that has drifted over time.

example.hanzi: 你今晚有空吗?我们能聊聊吗?
example.pinyin: Nǐ jīnwǎn yǒukòng ma? Wǒmen néng liáoliao ma?
example.english: Are you free tonight? Can we talk?
example.fact: 有空 literally means "to have (有) emptiness, free space (空)" — treating free time as an open, unoccupied slot in one's schedule, much like English "I have an opening." Its negation is simply 没有空, usually contracted to 没空.

components.note: 一 (one) — relates to 百's meaning 'hundred,' a large round number built from 'one.'
白 (bái) gives a sound hint — 百 is pronounced bǎi, sharing the same base sound with a different tone.

example.hanzi: 这家公司的营业额超过一百万。
example.pinyin: Zhè jiā gōngsī de yíngyè'é chāoguò yì bǎiwàn.
example.english: This company's revenue exceeds one million.
example.fact: The Chinese numbering system groups by four digits (万 "ten-thousand," 亿 "hundred-million") rather than English's three-digit groupings. 百万 ("hundred-万") is one of the few big numbers with a word matching Western "million," while native counting more naturally jumps straight from 万 to 亿.

components.note: 木 (wood) — buildings were traditionally framed with wood.
娄 (lóu) gives the sound — an exact match with 楼.
木 (wood) shows 梯 is typically made of wood.
弟 (dì) gives a sound close to tī, sharing a similar consonant sound though the vowel differs.

example.hanzi: 请走楼梯,电梯坏了。
example.pinyin: Qǐng zǒu lóutī, diàntī huài le.
example.english: Please take the stairs, the elevator is broken.
example.fact: 楼梯 and 电梯 ("elevator," literally "electric-梯") both end in 梯, a character built around 木 ("wood") depicting a ladder. The same root distinguishes a plain staircase ("building-ladder") from its modern electric counterpart just by swapping the first character.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — 呼 describes an action of the mouth, such as calling out or breathing.
乎 (hū) gives the sound — an exact match with 呼.
口 (mouth) — relates directly to 叫's meaning 'to call out, shout; to be named.'
丩 (jiū) served as the phonetic base; its pronunciation has since drifted well away from jiào.

example.hanzi: 飞行员通过无线电呼叫塔台。
example.pinyin: Fēixíngyuán tōngguò wúxiàndiàn hūjiào tǎtái.
example.english: The pilot called the control tower over the radio.
example.fact: 呼叫 stacks two "call out" verbs (呼, as in 呼喊; 叫, as in 叫喊) into one word. In the 20th century it picked up a specialized technical sense for calling over radio, telephone, or intercom (呼叫中心, "call center") — the older literal "to shout" sense and the newer telecom sense now coexist.

components.note: 凡 (common/ordinary) — suggests something shared or held in common.
口 (mouth) — sharing a common mouth/voice with others gave 同 its meaning of 'same, together.'
忄 (heart) — 情 relates to feelings and emotions.
青 (qīng) gives the sound — 情 is pronounced qíng, a close match differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 我很同情他的遭遇。
example.pinyin: Wǒ hěn tóngqíng tā de zāoyù.
example.english: I really sympathize with what happened to him.
example.fact: 同情 literally means "same (同) feeling (情)" — sharing another person's emotional state. That's the same root logic behind English "sympathy" (Greek syn- "together" + pathos "feeling"), a case where the Chinese and English etymologies for an abstract emotion line up almost exactly.

components.note: ⺼ (flesh/body) — 背 refers to the back, a part of the body
北 (běi) gives a sound close to 背's reading bèi, sharing a similar historical pronunciation
日 (the sun) — sunlight falling over the land
京 (a capital city) — a grand city view worth seeing

example.hanzi: 请介绍一下这个故事的背景。
example.pinyin: Qǐng jièshào yíxià zhège gùshi de bèijǐng.
example.english: Please introduce the background of this story.
example.fact: 背景 literally means "back (背) scenery (景)" — a term from theater staging and photography for whatever sits behind the main subject. It extended figuratively to mean both narrative "context" and, colloquially, a person's powerful hidden connections (有背景, "to have backing").

components.note: A short stroke placed below a longer one — the mirror image of 上 (up), together forming a simple, opposite pair.
王 here is a variant of 玉 (jade), appearing once on each side of the character.
刂 (knife) — cutting a piece of jade in two, symbolizing a division into groups, gave 班 its meaning 'class, group.'

example.hanzi: 我们通常六点下班。
example.pinyin: Wǒmen tōngcháng liù diǎn xiàbān.
example.english: We usually get off work at six o'clock.
example.fact: 下班 and 上班 ("to go to work") form a matched pair built on 班 ("shift, duty period" — the same 班 as in 班级, "school class"), with the directional opposites 上 ("up, into") and 下 ("down, out of") marking entering versus leaving one's post.

components.note: 比 is made of two identical 匕 (spoon) shapes placed side by side — comparing two similar things led to its meaning 'to compare.'
女 (woman) — depicts a wife in the traditional image behind this character.
口 (mouth/words) — the wife following her husband's spoken words gave 如 its meaning of 'as, like, if.'
讠 (speech radical) — shows 说 relates to talking or language
兑 (duì) is the phonetic component; historically 说 was also pronounced closer to 兑's sound before shifting to shuō

example.hanzi: 有很多方法可以学中文,比如说看电视剧。
example.pinyin: Yǒu hěn duō fāngfǎ kěyǐ xué Zhōngwén, bǐrúshuō kàn diànshìjù.
example.english: There are many ways to learn Chinese, for example watching TV dramas.
example.fact: 比如说 tacks 说 ("to say") onto the simpler 比如 ("for example," itself from 比 "to compare" + 如 "as, like"). The two are functionally interchangeable — adding 说 just gives the phrase a slightly more spoken, conversational feel, similar to how English sometimes adds "say" as in "let's say, for example."

components.note: 纟 (thread) — 绝 originally meant to sever a thread completely, extended to mean 'to cut off, absolute'
色 (sè) gives a loose sound connection to 绝's reading jué
Depicts a person standing tall, gazing up at the moon 月 — the image of looking into the distance, the source of 望's meaning 'to gaze, hope, expect.'

example.hanzi: 失去工作后,他感到很绝望。
example.pinyin: Shīqù gōngzuò hòu, tā gǎndào hěn juéwàng.
example.english: After losing his job, he felt very hopeless.
example.fact: 绝望 literally means "severed (绝) hope (望)." 绝 originally described cutting a thread completely through, so 绝望 pictures hope itself being cut clean through — a vivid escalation beyond just "having no hope" to hope being severed entirely.

components.note: 氵 (water/stream) — water naturally follows a fixed course, an image linked to the idea of 'law' or 'method.'
去 (to go/a course) — the path a stream follows suggested a regulated, consistent way of doing things, hence 'law, method.'
讠 (speech) — 语 relates to language, words, and speech
吾 (wú) gives a loose sound connection to 语's reading yǔ

example.hanzi: 她在大学学习法语。
example.pinyin: Tā zài dàxué xuéxí Fǎyǔ.
example.english: She studies French at university.
example.fact: 法语 abbreviates 法国 ("France") down to just 法 before adding 语 ("language") — the same one-character-country pattern seen throughout Chinese language names, e.g. 英语 (英 from 英国), 德语 (德 from 德国, also in this batch via 西德), and 俄语 (俄 from 俄罗斯, also in this batch).

components.note: 攵 (a hand taking action) — 救 describes the act of rescuing someone.
求 (qiú) gives a sound close to jiù, sharing a similar rhyme.
扌 (hand) — represents the act of guarding or defending.
户 (door/household) — protecting one's home gave 护 its meaning 'to protect, guard.'
A simplified form of 車, a pictograph of a two-wheeled cart seen from above — the wheels, axle, and frame are visible in the original shape — the source of 车's meaning 'cart, vehicle.'

example.hanzi: 请叫一辆救护车!
example.pinyin: Qǐng jiào yí liàng jiùhùchē!
example.english: Please call an ambulance!
example.fact: 救护车 is fully compositional: 救 ("to rescue," as in 救命 "help!") + 护 ("to protect, to nurse," as in 护士 "nurse") + 车 ("vehicle") — literally "rescue-and-care vehicle," a transparent three-character compound for a modern invention with no single native word before cars existed.

components.note: 入 (enter, put away) — 全 pictures something being placed into safekeeping.
玉 (jade) — a valuable treasure kept whole and undamaged, giving 全 its meaning of 'complete' or 'entire.'
亲 (here representing a tree, related to 榛/hazel) — 新 pictures a tree being cut.
斤 (an axe) — freshly chopping wood gave 新 its meaning of something 'new' or 'fresh.'

example.hanzi: 这是一款全新的手机。
example.pinyin: Zhè shì yì kuǎn quánxīn de shǒujī.
example.english: This is a brand-new phone.
example.fact: 全新 intensifies 新 ("new") with 全 ("whole, entire") to mean "completely/brand new" — parallel to how English "brand-new" adds an intensifying word rather than leaning on "new" alone, a common Mandarin strategy for emphasis alongside totality words like 十分 or 完全.

components.note: 西 is thought to depict a bird settling into its nest at dusk — since birds return to roost as the sun sets in the west, the character came to mean 'west.'
心 (heart/mind) — 德 relates to inner moral character and virtue.

example.hanzi: 他的父母出生在西德。
example.pinyin: Tā de fùmǔ chūshēng zài Xī Dé.
example.english: His parents were born in West Germany.
example.fact: 西德 is a Cold War-era term for the Federal Republic of Germany (1949–1990), paired with its counterpart 东德 ("East Germany," the GDR). Since German reunification in 1990 both terms have become historical rather than current — modern Mandarin simply uses 德国 for unified Germany.

components.note: 讠 (speech radical) — shows 说 relates to talking or language
兑 (duì) is the phonetic component; historically 说 was also pronounced closer to 兑's sound before shifting to shuō
讠 (speech radical) — shows 说 relates to talking or language
兑 (duì) is the phonetic component; historically 说 was also pronounced closer to 兑's sound before shifting to shuō

example.hanzi: 你能说说你的想法吗?
example.pinyin: Nǐ néng shuōshuo nǐ de xiǎngfǎ ma?
example.english: Can you tell me a bit about your thoughts?
example.fact: 说说 reduplicates 说 ("to speak") in the AA pattern Mandarin uses for brief, low-commitment actions — the same pattern behind 看看 ("take a quick look") and 想想 ("think it over"). Reduplicating the verb softens a request, turning a bare imperative "speak!" into a gentler "just say a little."

components.note: 氵 (water) — the radical here, though 沮's meaning has shifted well away from water.
且 (qiě) gives a sound distantly related to 沮's reading jǔ, having drifted apart over time.
哭 (to cry) — the top of the simplified character keeps the idea of crying in mourning.
亡 (dead, gone) — combined with crying above it, the image of weeping over the dead gave 丧 its meaning 'mourning, funeral.'

example.hanzi: 考试没考好让他很沮丧。
example.pinyin: Kǎoshì méi kǎohǎo ràng tā hěn jǔsàng.
example.english: Not doing well on the exam made him very dejected.
example.fact: 沮丧 pairs 沮 (whose 氵 water radical no longer connects clearly to dejection) with 丧, whose upper element pictures crying in mourning (from 哭). That mourning imagery anchors 沮丧's meaning a step beyond ordinary sadness, closer to a defeated, hope-drained gloom.

components.note: 木 (wood) — early models and molds were often carved from wood
莫 (mò) gives a sound close to 模's reading mó, sharing a similar historical pronunciation
亻 (person) — 仿 describes one person copying another.
方 (fāng) gives a sound close to fǎng, differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 小孩子喜欢模仿父母的行为。
example.pinyin: Xiǎo háizi xǐhuan mófǎng fùmǔ de xíngwéi.
example.english: Small children like to imitate their parents' behavior.
example.fact: 模仿 combines 模 ("mold, pattern," as in 模型 "model/mockup") with 仿 ("to copy, to resemble," as in 仿佛 "as if") — literally "to copy a mold," a concrete image standing in for the abstract act of imitation.

components.note: 户 (door) — 所 evokes a location or place, such as where a door stands.
斤 (axe) — combined with 户 (door), the image of an axe at a door gave rise to the abstract sense of 'a place' or 'that which.'

example.hanzi: 我爸爸在一家律师事务所工作。
example.pinyin: Wǒ bàba zài yì jiā lǜshī shìwùsuǒ gōngzuò.
example.english: My dad works at a law firm.
example.fact: 事务所 almost always attaches to a profession — most commonly 律师事务所 ("law firm," literally "lawyer affairs-office") and 会计师事务所 ("accounting firm"). It rarely stands alone in speech, functioning more like a suffix template for professional-services firms than a freestanding word for "office," for which 办公室 is the everyday term.

components.note: 宀 (a roof) — a house.
火 (fire) — burning inside it, together giving 灾 its meaning 'disaster, calamity.'
又 (a hand) — reaching out to try to catch something.
隹 (a bird) — catching a bird by hand is hard, giving 难 its meaning 'difficult.'

example.hanzi: 这场洪水是一场巨大的灾难。
example.pinyin: Zhè chǎng hóngshuǐ shì yì chǎng jùdà de zāinàn.
example.english: This flood is a huge disaster.
example.fact: 灾难 combines 灾 (fire 火 breaking out under a roof 宀, per its own component breakdown) with 难 (originally "hard to catch a bird by hand," per its own component breakdown) — two independently vivid pictographic images of calamity reinforcing each other into one formal word for disaster.

components.note: 爫 (a hand, claw-like) — reaching to pick something.
木 (tree) — a hand picking fruit from a tree gave 采 its meaning 'to pick, gather, collect.'
讠 (speech) — 访 relates to visiting someone to speak with them or ask questions.
方 (fāng) gives a sound distantly related to fǎng, having drifted apart over time.

example.hanzi: 记者采访了这位科学家。
example.pinyin: Jìzhě cǎifǎng le zhè wèi kēxuéjiā.
example.english: The reporter interviewed this scientist.
example.fact: 采访 combines 采 ("to pick, to gather," pictured as a hand picking fruit from a tree) with 访 ("to visit, to call on") — journalism here is pictured as "gathering by visiting," a concrete metaphor for a reporter's fieldwork that predates the modern sense "to interview."

components.note: 讠 (speech) — 评 relates to speaking judgments or opinions about something
平 (píng) gives the sound — an exact match with 评's reading píng
介 (jiè) gives a sound hint — 价 is pronounced jià, sharing the same initial consonant though the vowel has shifted.

example.hanzi: 老师对他的作文评价很高。
example.pinyin: Lǎoshī duì tā de zuòwén píngjià hěn gāo.
example.english: The teacher rated his essay very highly.
example.fact: 评价 combines 评 ("to comment, to judge," as in 评论 "commentary") with 价 ("value, price," as in 价格 "price") — literally "to judge the value of." English "to appraise" carries the same logic, tracing back to Latin appretiare, "to set a price on."
